subject: chemistry
question_text: Define enthalpy of neutralisation. What is its value for a strong acid and a strong base?

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This question comes from the enumeration sweep of the Thermodynamics syllabus: the book's SAQ 3 covers formation, fusion, vapourisation, sublimation and combustion but skips neutralisation entirely, a standard enthalpy type in the syllabus. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry, so the two-book union check is PENDING — a second source may show this asked. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: change when one mole of H⁺ ions from an
acid reacts with one mole of OH⁻ ions from
a base in dilute solution, forming one
steps.why: Fixing the amount at one mole of water formed makes values from different acid-base pairs comparable.
common_mistakes: Defining it per mole of acid instead of per mole of H⁺ reacting — for H₂SO₄ the two differ.
steps.memory_tip: One mole of H⁺ meets one mole of OH⁻ and one mole of water forms — three ones in one definition.
steps.margin_note: Dilute solution and one mole of water are the checked phrases.

steps.label: The value and its reason
lines: For any strong acid with any strong base
the value is the same, because both are
fully ionised and the only reaction is
steps.why: Strong acids and bases are completely ionised in dilute solution, so whichever pair is chosen, the chemical change is the same one reaction between H⁺ and OH⁻. A weak acid or base gives a smaller release, because part of the heat goes into ionising it first.
common_mistakes: Writing the value without the minus sign — neutralisation releases heat.
Claiming the same constant value for weak acids — it holds only when both are strong.
steps.memory_tip: Strong plus strong is always the same reaction, so always the same number: −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps.margin_note: The constancy argument is the understanding the examiner checks.
